text.text: An employee needs extended time off for medical, family, personal, or other reasons. Different leave types carry different legal protections. Getting the leave type wrong is a common and costly error.

• An employee requesting 6 weeks off following a surgery with a slow recovery.
• A team member needing intermittent leave to care for a parent with a chronic illness.
• An employee who has exhausted PTO and is asking for unpaid leave due to a mental health condition.
• A new parent requesting leave beyond what the company's paid policy covers.
• An employee called to active military duty requiring extended absence.
• A team member experiencing a pregnancy complication requiring immediate time off.
• An employee requesting leave to care for a seriously ill child or spouse.
• Someone requesting a personal leave of absence for reasons unrelated to a medical condition.
Gather and preserve these records as you work through the check.

1. Record the date the employee first communicated the need for leave — even informally.
2. Document which leave type(s) apply and the basis for that determination.
3. Log all paperwork sent and received, including dates and delivery method.
4. Keep a record of any medical certifications, including when they were requested and received.
5. Document the return-to-work date, any extensions granted, and whether an accommodation review was conducted.

elements.text: You can attach files and links securely from the completed assessment before submitting it to HR.

text.text: Watch for: Assuming a leave request is just a 'time off' issue. Many leaves trigger FMLA, ADA, state leave law, or all three simultaneously.
Contact HR: If you are not certain which leave law applies — or if the employee has a medical condition involved in any way — contact HR before responding to the request.
